One of the world’s leading independent biotechnology companies faced a major compliance challenge with cybersecurity vulnerabilities across its global Quality Control (QC) laboratories. A comprehensive vulnerability assessment revealed that 93% of 596 benchtop systems were operating on outdated systems or unsupported software, creating over 6,300 security vulnerabilities. Further, these instruments were not consistently connected to the Manufacturing (MFG) network, limiting centralized oversight, patch management, and data backup. The fragmented environment increased the risk of malware propagation, production downtime, and compliance issues. ### **USDM Solution**. results.title: Effect of quality control program on surgical management in ...
results.content: doi: 10.3802/jgo.2025.36.e21 Effect of quality control program on surgical management in advanced ovarian cancer ### Bo Ra Kim 1 Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Ewha Womans University College of Medicine, Seoul, Korea. ### Objective We investigated the effect of our quality control (QC) program on the management strategy, completeness of the surgery, and clinical outcomes in advanced ovarian cancer. In this study, we aim to evaluate the effect of our QC program on management strategy, completeness of the surgery and clinical outcomes in advanced ovarian cancer. We evaluated the effect of an institutional and systemic QC program on management strategy, surgical completeness, and clinical outcomes for advanced ovarian cancer, with the aim of improving treatment outcomes. The quality and completeness of surgical treatment have a significant impact on the clinical outcomes of advanced ovarian cancer patients [7,8,18]. [24] examined the effects of a quality management program on advanced ovarian cancer patients, categorizing 396 patients who underwent primary surgery for the disease into three groups: before the program’s implementation, during its implementation period, and after it had been established. Unfortunately, apart from Harter’s study, very few other studies have directly evaluated the impact of implementing a systematic quality management program in the surgical care of patients with advanced ovarian cancer. In our study, despite statistically no significant differences in patient characteristics, such as stage or histology, between groups 1 and 2, the selection of PDS as the initial treatment for advanced ovarian cancer patients decreased after the introduction of the quality program. The improvement of the optimal resection rate in the PDS group and the maintenance of a consistently high optimal resection rate in the IDS group can be seen as suggesting that our QC program has consistently emphasized the importance of minimizing residual lesions through advanced procedures and more aggressive collaborative surgery with other departments in the surgical treatment of advanced ovarian cancer. Importantly, despite the increase in aggressive surgical procedures aimed at achieving complete cytoreduction, influenced by the QC program that aims to provide optimal treatment and care for ovarian cancer patients, the rates of intra- and post-operative complications did not show a statistically significant increase, and the overall length of hospital stay after surgery was reduced.

Finding the best subgroup with differential treatment effect with multiple outcomes Beibo Zhao1,Jason Fine2,Anastasia Ivanova1 ### Affiliations * 1 Department of Biostatistics, CB #7420, The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, USA. * DOI: 10.1002/sim.10083 Finding the best subgroup with differential treatment effect with multiple outcomes . Existing definitions for the best subgroup in subgroup analysis are based on a single outcome and do not consider multiple outcomes; specifically, outcomes of different types. In this article, we introduce a definition for the best subgroup under a multiple-outcome setting with continuous, binary, and censored time-to-event outcomes. Our definition provides a trade-off between the subgroup size and the conditional average treatment effects (CATE) in the subgroup with respect to each of the outcomes while taking the relative contribution of the outcomes into account. **Keywords:** cross‐validation; multiple outcomes; predictive biomarker; subgroup analysis; treatment effect heterogeneity. © 2024 John Wiley & Sons Ltd.
